newsitem.title: USA: Wheat prices climb as USDA cut stocks projections.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices climb as USDA cut stocks projections.

text.p: Wheat prices jumped Tuesday as the Department of Agriculture cut estimates of domestic and world stockpiles while soybean prices climbed despite an improved crop outlook.
In New York, gasoline prices rose on concern about tight supplies, but crude and heating oil drifted lower in quiet trading.
The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures fell 0.15 point to 240.49.
"World (wheat) stocks were cut, U.S. stocks were cut and that prompted some (buying)," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures.
The department in its November report trimmed to 435 million bushels, from 470 million bushels previously, its estimate for domestic stockpiles of wheat for the marketing year ending on May 31.
The department trimmed its estimate of world stockpiles to 110.8 million metric tons from 116.5 million tons in the October report.
Traders said the news should help halt the drop in wheat prices on the Chicago Board of Trade from a high of $7.50 a bushel in March to a 17-month low of $3.66 earlier this month.
"The wheat market is stabilising worldwide," Searcy said.
Wheat for December delivery rose 8 cents to $3.91-1/2 a bushel at the CBOT.
The department also raised its U.S. soybean production estimate by 57 million bushels to 2.40 billion bushels, which would be the second biggest crop ever.
Upward revisions to soybean export and domestic demand projections, however, sparked gains in futures. November soybeans rose 8-1/2 cents to $6.88-1/2 a bushel, also at the CBOT.
"People are impressed by the demand for soybeans," Karlin said Everen Securities analyst Joel Karlin.
Gasoline rose on concerns of tight supplies, while crude and heating oil drifted lower in thin trading as traders awaited weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API).
"There is a perception that gasoline supplies are tight. There has been strong buying in the cash markets," said a trader.
Gasoline's gains were concentrated in the December contract, the nearest month for delivery, reflecting fears that current stocks were not adequate, one trader said.

Gasoline for December delivery rose 0.75 cent to 65.77 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. December crude oil fell 2 cents to $23.35 a barrel and December heating oil settled 0.10 cent lower at 68.25 cents a gallon.
The API was scheduled to report its weekly oil inventory data late Tuesday but it said it would delay the report until Wednesday afternoon.
An API spokesman said not enough companies had reported data after Monday's Veteran's Day holiday to produce the report on Tuesday.
In the the most recent inventory data for the week ended Nov. 1, gasoline stocks were 6.2 million barrels below year-ago levels and hovered near record lows.
"The market is going to be looking at the APIs to confirm the move in gasoline," said one trader.
Meanwhile, forecasts of moderating temperatures for the U.S. Northeast starting Friday weighed on heating oil prices, which in turn pressured crude.
